Repress

/rih-PRES/ - rhymes with dress · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Repress means to hold something down by force, or to push an unwanted feeling or memory out of your own mind.

The junta repressed even mourning, posting soldiers at the cemetery gates on each anniversary of the massacre.

Worked Example

In 1848 the kingdom's reformers discovered that dinner was illegal. Political meetings were banned, so the opposition held banquets instead — toasts as speeches, menus as manifestos — until the crown saw through the tablecloths. Gatherings of more than twenty now required a permit; permits were never granted; and the cavalry learned the address of every hall in the capital that could seat a hundred.

Repress is the exact word for the crown's answer, because to repress is to hold something down by force — the banquets did not end because appetites changed. Restrain, this unit's gentler cousin, holds a thing back to keep it under control; repress puts the state's whole weight on top of it and sits.

How Repress Sits Among Its Neighbors

Antonyms

permit

How Strong Is It? — curb → repress → crush

curb vs. repress

curb vs. repress: Curb is the light rein — a rule that trims a habit's edges and leaves the habit alive.

crush vs. repress

crush vs. repress: Crush goes further than repress — a repressed movement survives underground, waiting; a crushed one is gone.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back, down

Root — press

Root — press: to press (Latin premere, pressare)

Put it together

Put it together: Re- (back, down) + press = to press back down. Latin reprimere did exactly this — pressed a thing back whenever it rose — and English kept the physics: whatever is repressed is still pushing upward, which is why it takes standing force, and why it so often returns the moment the weight lifts.

Use the root in a new word: pressure

Use the root in a new word: pressure: Pressure is the same root as plain noun — the bearing-down force itself, whether on a valve or a witness.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / political

Repress is the historian's verb for force from above: strikes, uprisings, and mourning get repressed, and so — in the mind's own police state — do memories and feelings. Restrain is protective or neutral, a hold rather than a weight; impede merely slows; and the same crackdown done with licenses and ledgers instead of cavalry usually goes by suppression.
